oneness_pentecostal.trinity:
Oneness Pentecostals teach the oneness of God: there is one God, not three persons, and this one God has revealed himself in different ways. Father, Son and Holy Spirit are understood as titles or manifestations of the one God, as he has acted in creation, in redemption and in the believer's life. They therefore do not accept the traditional doctrine of the Trinity.

Their teaching is based on passages such as the declaration that the Lord our God is one, and on the New Testament's identification of Jesus with God. Oneness Pentecostals believe that all the fullness of the Godhead dwells in Jesus. They generally prefer words like manifestation or role over the word persons, and they are aware that most other Christians consider the Trinity essential, so they explain their teaching carefully from Scripture.
oneness_pentecostal.father:
For Oneness Pentecostals, Father is a title of the one God, and not the name of a separate person alongside the Son. God is Father in that he is the creator and the source of all things, and Father to his people. Jesus is not another person distinct from the Father, but the same God who is Father, revealed in human flesh.

Oneness believers read passages in which Jesus speaks of the Father as referring to the deity dwelling in the human nature of Jesus, and as distinguishing the divine and human aspects of the one person of Christ. This differs from the traditional view that the Father and the Son are two eternally distinct persons. Members find in this teaching a way of honoring the unity of God as the Bible declares it.
oneness_pentecostal.holy_spirit:
Oneness Pentecostals speak of the Holy Ghost, or the Spirit of God, and understand it not as a third person distinct from the Father and the Son but as the one God himself in action, especially as he works in the human heart and dwells in the believer. God is spirit, and the Holy Ghost is the same God who is Father and who came in Jesus.

For this reason the coming of the Holy Ghost into a person's life is understood as God himself coming to live within. It is a central part of the Oneness understanding of salvation, and they expect it to be evident in a life of holiness and in speaking in tongues. This differs from the Trinitarian understanding of the Holy Spirit as a distinct person, and members are accustomed to explaining the difference.
oneness_pentecostal.name_of_god:
Oneness Pentecostals teach that Jesus is the name of the one God in his redemptive work: the name given to the Father's manifestation in the Son, and the name above every name. They point to New Testament passages where healings, miracles, prayer, baptism and teaching are done in the name of Jesus.

For them, to speak of the name of Jesus is to speak of God's own name for the age of salvation. It is used in worship, in prayer, in blessing and above all in baptism, where the name is spoken over the person being baptized. Members regard this as more than a formula, since to call on the name of Jesus is to call on God himself. Other Christians who hold that Jesus is a distinct person of the Trinity understand the significance of the name differently.
oneness_pentecostal.natures_of_christ:
Oneness Pentecostals teach that Jesus Christ is fully God and fully man: the one God manifested in the flesh, as the First Letter to Timothy puts it. In Jesus there is real deity, since he is the one God himself, and real humanity, with a human body, soul and will.

Many Oneness believers understand the title Son of God as referring especially to the humanity of Jesus, the flesh which the eternal God took on, while the deity dwelling in it is the Father. They generally do not speak of an eternal Son distinct from the Father, as the traditional doctrine does. They hold that the man Jesus was truly tempted and truly died, while the fullness of God dwelt in him. They see this as honoring both the humanity and the deity of Christ.
oneness_pentecostal.baptism_in_the_spiri:
Oneness Pentecostals teach that baptism in the Holy Ghost, evidenced by speaking in tongues, is part of the new birth, and not an optional experience after it. They draw on the account in the Acts of the Apostles where Peter tells the crowd to repent, be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ and receive the gift of the Holy Ghost.

In this understanding, the new birth consists of repentance, baptism in water in Jesus' name and baptism in the Spirit. Speaking in tongues is taught as the initial evidence that a person has received the Holy Ghost. The gift is promised to every believer, and members are encouraged to seek it in prayer. Emphasis differs somewhat among Oneness organizations, but this pattern of three parts is central to their teaching about salvation.
oneness_pentecostal.tongues:
Oneness Pentecostals speak in tongues, and most teach that this is the initial evidence of receiving the Holy Ghost. Following the accounts in Acts, they expect that a person who is filled with the Spirit will speak in a language given by the Spirit, which the speaker has not learned.

Tongues are also used as a prayer language and, with interpretation, as a gift in the assembly. Oneness teaching treats tongues as an expected sign that the Holy Ghost has come and as a mark of the new birth. Other Pentecostals hold that tongues are a sign of the baptism of the Spirit that is separate from salvation, and other Christians do not expect it at all. Oneness believers stress that it is a gift from God and not something a person can produce.
oneness_pentecostal.repentance:
Repentance is the first step in the Oneness Pentecostal understanding of how a person receives salvation. It means a real turning from sin toward God, with sorrow for wrongdoing and a decision to change one's life. It is not a matter of feeling regret only, but of a change of direction.

Following the apostle Peter's words in Acts, repentance leads to baptism in Jesus' name and to the receiving of the Holy Ghost. Members believe that repentance continues throughout the Christian life as the believer turns from sin again and again in obedience to God. It is a gift of God's grace and a response to it, and it prepares the person for the rest of the new birth.
oneness_pentecostal.baptism:
Oneness Pentecostals baptize in the name of Jesus Christ, for the remission of sins, following the pattern they read in the book of Acts. They understand baptism as an essential part of the new birth, and as the point at which sins are washed away when the person is baptized in faith.

They teach that the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit in the command of Jesus is the one name of Jesus, and so they do not use the trinitarian formula when baptizing. Other Christians who baptize in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit generally understand baptism differently, and Oneness believers are aware that they are often told their baptism differs from what others practice.
oneness_pentecostal.mode_of_baptism:
Oneness Pentecostals baptize by immersion: the whole person is placed under the water, in the name of Jesus Christ. They understand this as picturing burial and resurrection with Christ, as taught in the Letter to the Romans, and they follow the pattern they see in the New Testament.

Baptism is given to those who repent and believe, and infants are not baptized. Sprinkling or pouring is not regarded as baptism. Members who were baptized in another way, or by another formula, are generally asked to be baptized again in Jesus' name when they join. This is not intended as a slight on their earlier faith but as obedience to what Oneness Pentecostals understand to be the biblical pattern.
oneness_pentecostal.foot_washing:
Some Oneness Pentecostal churches practice foot washing as an ordinance, following the example of Jesus in the Gospel of John, who washed his disciples' feet and told them to do the same. It is understood as an act of humility and service, and it is often performed as part of a communion service.

Practices differ among Oneness Pentecostal organizations and congregations. Some keep foot washing regularly, some occasionally, and some do not observe it as a formal ordinance. Where it is practiced, believers usually wash one another's feet in pairs, and it is regarded as a serious and moving act of fellowship. It is treated as a matter of obedience to Christ's example, and not as something that saves.
